source.title: Understanding Addition and Subtraction in Transformers
source.authors: P. Quirke; Clement Neo; Fazl Barez

record.tranche_reason: The study reports that mixed-operation nodes perform several related addition and subtraction subtasks, refining the scope of polysemanticity; it does not test whether unrelated input mixtures are common.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports circuit search, ablation, patching, and accuracy results, but those do not bear on the listed versions of the polysemanticity claim. The polysemanticity evidence concerns nodes in arithmetic models, not individual neurons in vision or language models.
record.test_reason: The paper calls attention heads and MLP-layer nodes in tiny arithmetic transformers 'polysemantic' because they compute related addition and subtraction subtasks at once. It does not measure individual neurons responding to unrelated inputs in vision or language models. It does not test superposition, capacity, architecture effects or measurement choices. It does not re-examine canonical polysemantic neurons with better tools. This is a related but different construct: multi-task reuse of circuit nodes. No version is tested, so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that mixed models reuse addition circuitry polysemantically for subtraction, whether or not initialized from an addition model. They call this reuse natural because the three operations share structure. Operation selection is distributed and high-dimensional, feeding a shared last-layer combiner.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses arithmetic subtask mapping, node counts, ablation, and causal patching rather than the original polysemantic-neuron examples or measurement.

fits_no_version.finding: In mixed arithmetic transformers, most attention-head and MLP nodes inherited from an addition model come to compute addition, positive- and negative-answer subtraction outputs simultaneously. In one sample model, 42 of 48 inserted nodes serve addition. The paper says such reuse also arises when training from scratch.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Circuit nodes (heads/MLP layers) in small multi-task transformers are reused across structurally related subtasks ('polysemantic' multi-task reuse), rather than forming separate per-task circuits.

record.problems: The polysemanticity evidence is at the node level, which can include attention heads, MLP layers, or groups of heads, rather than individual neurons. The quantitative reuse table describes one sample mixed model; the paper does not report a prevalence of unrelated mixtures.
record.rows_left_out: No other polysemanticity results were reported separately in the text.

untested.parts: Vision classifiers and neurons responding to unrelated images: not studied.
MLP neurons in language models responding to unrelated tokens or contexts: not studied. The models are 2–4 layer arithmetic transformers, analysed at node level.
Superposition and feature-versus-neuron capacity: not studied.
Polysemanticity from initialization, regularization or noise without capacity pressure: not studied. The initialization experiments concern transfer of addition circuits, not neuron polysemanticity.
Effect of activation function, architecture or regularization on the share of polysemantic neurons: not studied.
Re-examination of canonical polysemantic neurons, and the rarity of truly unrelated mixtures: not studied.
Dependence on activation range or explanation scoring: not studied.

record.verdict_notes: 'Polysemantic' is used in a task-reuse sense at the level of heads and MLP layers, not individual neurons. All evidence comes from ~10M-parameter arithmetic models. The reader's V6 'supports' label should be dropped: related-subtask reuse of nodes does not show that canonical polysemantic neurons were misread.

versions.untested_parts: Transformer language-model MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than available neurons.
Polysemanticity from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Effects of activation function, architecture, or regularization on polysemantic-neuron share and performance.
The study examines arithmetic nodes, not canonical individual neurons; it does not establish whether unrelated mixtures are rare in general or test the cited vision-neuron example.
How the measured prevalence of polysemanticity depends on activation range or explanation scoring.
